subject: Phylogenetic PCA and PaCA - statistical analyses

messages.author: 364b34b2b0ded261
messages.subject: Phylogenetic PCA and PaCA - statistical analyses
parts:
Hi all,

I have a question about the phylogenetic PCA (phyPCA) and phylogenetic aligned component analysis (PaCA). At this point, I'm using both to study shape variation in the ulna of different primate taxa. However, I'm a bit confused on how I can test for significant differences between groups. 

In a previous analysis in which I used a regular PCA, I used an ANCOVA to test for differences between the different primate species (e.g. cimpansee versus gibbon). But since I'm now working with mean shapes (to match the nodes of the phylogenetic tree to the datapoints), I can't run an ANCOVA because this would be like running a test on a sample size of 1. There is no variation, so it's not possible to run any statistical test between the species when using mean shapes only.

In the PaCA, I tried to project the individuals into the shape space. The phylogenetically aligned components are variables as any other, so it should be possible to run analysis to see how the species differ. However, there is still the issue about spurious groups ... I could try to fix this according to the paper of Thioulouse et al. 2021.

I've also read some information on a 'phylogenetic PCA', but I don't know for sure if this can be used when working with mean shapes. Other papers, for example Lewton 2015, don't use a phyPCA due to its efficacy in studies of adaptation (I also don't know how to map the individuals in the shape space here because of the transformation of the residuals), but they mapped a phylogeny onto the standard PCA to visualize the effect of phylogeny on morphology in the morphospace. Locomotor group differences in principal component scores were then investigated using pANOVA.

Could someone help me with clarifying what would be the best approach here?
Thank you for clearing this up for me.

Marie.

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic PCA and PaCA - statistical analyses
parts:
Marie,

 

As you noted, with phylogenetic comparative analyses one has 1 individual per species: the species average. That means that certain analyses simply are ‘off the table’. One cannot compare groups if there is no within-group variation, so if one wishes to compare shapes among species, and there is only 1 observation per species (the mean), that becomes problematic.


Dean
